stories.title: Winners & Sinners: Week 1
stories.summary: Who and what stood out in Milwaukee’s opening week?
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 24: Jaime Jaquez Jr. #24 of the Milwaukee Bucks looks on during the game against the Philadelphia 76ers on October 24, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Welcome to Winners & Sinners, our new weekly feature that reflects on the week that was. With Giannis wearing enemy colours and a new, youthful Bucks corps leading the charge, this season presents the unique opportunity to see just who is the Most Valuable Buck (MVB). But that’s not the only “award.” Each week, we’ll hand out the following: Defensive Belt : Ring the bells, this one’s a fight! Want to take home the belt? Get stops. But it’s more than just that. The “Defending Champion” wears the belt until a “Contender” takes it. The People’s Champ : Awarded to the Brew Hoop commenter of the week. Win it because of a wry comment in a game thread, an insightful fan post in The Feed , or simply in acknowledgement of all your hard work posting. It’s our shoutout to you. Run That Back : If this was a magazine, Run That Back would be a tear-out poster. It’s the highlight of the week. Sinner(s) : Think of this as Brew Hoop’s Razzies. It’s a chance for catharsis, calling out what needs it. If… Then… : A forward-looking conditional statement. If you continue to read this article, then you’ll see what I mean (please do). Now that you know the categories, let’s see the recipients! MVB It’s got to be Jaime Jaquez Jr., right? Tyler Herro has certainly put up a great argument, posting 23.7 PPG, 4.3 RPG, and 5.3 APG—and he’s quickly converting this writer into a fan. But after exploding against the Bulls he was relatively quiet against the 76ers. Meanwhile, Jaquez has been Milwaukee’s most consistent player. In addition to his 20.7 PPG (on 61% shooting!), Jaquez is contributing 8.7 RPG and 3.7 APG while playing with the sort of effort that Taylor Jenkins has preached all offseason. Defensive Belt Defending Champion : Vacant. The Contenders: Kyle Kuzma, Jaime Jaquez Jr. The Decision: Look, there haven’t exactly been any All-Defensive pushes to start the season, but the Bucks’ starting forwards have shown the most grunt (I’ll leave GRIT to retired janitor). Kyle Kuzma was the only semblance of a roadblock against Anthony Davis and has hit the glass hard , pulling down a team-leading 27 rebounds, including 21 on the defensive glass. He gets the nod. The People’s Champ naveed2000s takes the cake for this one, putting on a Woj Shams mask to drop news of the Golden State Warriors’ interest in trading Kristaps Porziņģis to the Bucks—before we could even think about getting a newser out. Kudos to you, naveed. Catch the scoop and join the conversation here: Run That Back Herro curls around a Myles Turner screen, catches and rises up—fluid, like Lake Michigan. Splash! And the harm. He converts on the two-to-make-one flagrant free throw too. It should’ve been the momentum moment to spur the Bucks to victory; the first of a long list in Herro’s Bucks lore. Instead, it’ll have to settle for this week’s highlight moment. Sinner(s) Meat Loaf said two out of three ain’t bad but in the NBA it’s a prerequisite—you need at least two of talent, smarts, or effort to truly succeed. At the moment, Ware has the talent. The know-how and the motor are works in progress. Thankfully, Jenkins is a teacher. Then again, so is Erik Spoelstra. The real question, then: does Ware know the difference between hearing and listening? If his performance against the 76ers is anything to go by, the answer is a resounding “Yes!” Myles Turner, on the other hand, has been flat-out bad —7.7 PPG and 4.3 RPG, shooting below 40% from the field—to go along with 3.0 turnovers per game, while coming last on the team in plus/minus (-11.0) and offering little in the way of a paint presence. It’s time to hit the confessional. Otherwise, the fourth quarters have been capital “R” Rough for the Bucks. Through three games, they’ve been outscored 98-73. Turn that around and they’d be sitting pretty. If… Then… If Ryan Rollins doesn’t start finding his offensive groove soon—which includes turning off the blinders so that he can run the team more effectively—then Taylor Jenkins might be wise to turn even more to Kasparas Jakučionis. The young Lithuanian has starting point guard written all over him. Did I win the tip or am I running back on defence? Share your winners and sinners in the comments.

stories.title: 76ers' Jaylen Brown claims no beef but says Jayson Tatum has 'hell of a PR team'
stories.summary: In the latest turn in the relationship between former teammates, Jaylen Brown said Jayson Tatum should "stay ready at all times" while denying the two have beef.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA -- The jagged relationship between former Boston Celtics teammates Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown took another turn Saturday night, when Brown insisted there was "no beef" between them but added that there "might be a little lamb chops and some gravy." "He should stay ready at all times," Brown said after scoring a season-high 27 points in the Philadelphia 76ers ' 127-116 win over the Milwaukee Bucks to improve to 3-0. Brown and Tatum played together in Boston for nine seasons. Both were the No. 3 picks, Brown in 2016 and Tatum a year later. Together, they were one of the most successful pairings of their era, guiding the Celtics to five Eastern Conference finals appearances, two NBA Finals trips and a championship win over the Dallas Mavericks in 2024. Despite that success, throughout their tenure, critics questioned the duo's ceiling. "I think we can play together," Brown said, defending the pairing in 2022. "We have played together well for the majority of our career." After their 2024 Finals win, donning Celtics championship T-shirts and hats while smiling, Tatum and Brown hugged at midcourt. Tatum yelled: "They said we couldn't play together!" Two years later, Brown, who was sent to the 76ers in a stunning offseason trade, and Tatum, still in Boston, have spent the past two days explaining what appears to be a strained relationship. Brown created a stir on social media earlier this week by posting a blue hat emoji -- a symbol for "cap," which is slang for someone lying -- on Instagram in response to Tatum saying in a video on his YouTube channel that he was "just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world" by Brown's trade. "There's no beef. It's not about that. It should be more praise," Tatum said Friday night. "I understand drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really into that. I'm not blaming everybody for how they feel. Everybody is entitled to their own feelings, and we all go through different things in our lives." ​There have been indications that Brown and Tatum weren't the best of friends this offseason. Ahead of the Sixers' preseason matchup against the Celtics in Boston two weeks ago, Brown and Tatum worked out pregame on opposite sides of the court and didn't appear to acknowledge each other. ​On Saturday, Brown repeated that there was no beef but that Tatum had a great public relations team. ​Brown declined to address why he posted the cap emoji under Tatum's post, instead saying he and Tatum are focused on what's ahead. Tatum said he would welcome a conversation with Brown to hash out the potential issue. Asked if he would be open to that conversation, Brown appeared to be disinterested. "We both got so much stuff in front of us," Brown said. "So at the end of the day ... he gotta do what he's got to do for his team. I gotta do what I do for my team. ​"Jayson's a great guy. Like I said, great family, hell of a basketball player, hell of a PR team. There's no beef, but it'll be a little lamb chop." Brown, who turned 30 on Saturday, was a five-time All-Star in Boston as well as the 2024 Eastern Conference finals and NBA Finals MVP in helping the Celtics win their 18th championship. He was coming off the best season of his career in 2025-26, stepping up while Tatum was sidelined for all but 16 games as he recovered from an Achilles rupture. With Tatum out, Brown finished sixth in MVP voting last season and was a second-team All-NBA selection while leading the Celtics to 56 wins. He averaged 28.7 points, 6.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists per game. ​Still, the Celtics moved forward with Tatum, sending Brown to Philadelphia for Paul George , two first-round picks (2028, 2031) and two second-round selections (2028, 2030). "I'm still processing how this all went down. I'm excited and disappointed at the same time," Brown said in a statement on social media after the trade. Brown and Tatum will face off for the first time Nov. 10, when the Sixers play the Celtics in Philadelphia.

stories.title: Suns overcome defensive lapses to win home opener against Warriors
stories.summary: A win over a depleted Warriors roster provided relief, but Phoenix still has plenty to prove.
stories.detailText: PHOENIX, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 24: Will Richard #3 of the Golden State Warriors pressures Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns during the second half at Mortgage Matchup Center on October 24, 2026 in Phoenix, Arizona. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images A win is a win, and in the NBA, they can be hard to come by. You take them however you can get them, up to and including when the opposing team decides to sit the majority of its roster. That’s how the Phoenix Suns earned their first win of the season in their home opener, and it ended up being a pretty important one when you consider they have the Thunder and Nuggets on the schedule next week. Starting 0-2 and heading into those matchups would’ve added even more pressure to a team that’s still trying to figure out who it is. Because that’s where we are right now, isn’t it? We knew who the Suns were last season. We don’t know who this version of the team is yet. While continuity remains, there’s still plenty of room for players to learn where their teammates are going to be and how they’re going to operate together on both ends of the floor. We witnessed that multiple times Saturday night against the Warriors. Countless defensive rotations were missed, leading to wide-open shooters. Lackadaisical inbound passes resulted in turnovers. And rebounding? Oh boy, it appears that’s going to be a significant issue for this team throughout the season. When you’re surrendering 16 offensive rebounds to what essentially amounts to the Santa Cruz Warriors, that’s not a talent issue. That’s a size issue. The undersized Suns were getting owned on the glass by a team considered one of the smallest in the NBA. In fact, per Salary Swish , Golden State is the shortest team in the league, while Phoenix sits right in the middle at 17th. It certainly didn’t feel that way Saturday night. They say you can’t truly know who and what a team is until 20 games into the season, and I believe that. But I also believe each game leading up to that 20-game mark serves as a little quiz, giving us another opportunity to understand the attitude and aptitude of a team. The good news from Saturday night is that the Phoenix Suns won. Their star stepped up and performed like one, and the team shot the basketball well. Collectively, Phoenix shot 37.8% from beyond the arc and 58.1% from the field. For a team that was anemic offensively against the Portland Trail Blazers, that’s an encouraging sign and a step in the right direction. Defensively? Allowing 122 points to that version of the Warriors is concerning. Getting outrebounded 19–9 on the offensive glass is equally troubling, as is being outscored 26–9 in second-chance points. So we’ll continue compiling the results of these little quizzes over the next 20 games until we have a clearer understanding of what this version of the Phoenix Suns looks like. Because we knew what last season looked like. And thus far this season? It ain’t that. Bright Side Baller Standings The season opener left us with but one real option as the Bright Side Baller. And true to form, the community stepped up and got the vote right. That winner? Mariah Carey. She has become our beacon when everything else is dark, for her 5-octave vocal range is that of a Hero. It’s no Fantasy that Anytime You Need a Friend, after dealing with a Heartbreaker like the Suns did against Portland, she’ll help with those Emotions. stories.detailText: The game turned out to be more of an adventure than seemed likely when the Wizards took a 21-point lead early in the fourth quarter, but they prevailed in the end, outlasting the Chicago Bulls, 124-120, for their first road win of the season. The Wizards built that lead with a heady third quarter blitz in which they outscored the Bulls 40-20. After falling behind by 21, the Bulls cut into Washington’s lead, but the Wizards maintained what seemed to be a comfortable double-digit advantage. Chicago rallied over the final three minutes. Washington’s lead dwindled to as little as three points with 23 seconds to play. Justin Champagnie corralled 14 rebounds in 26 minutes. | Getty Images Trae Young and Anthony Davis made their free throws at the end to ice the game and escape the Windy City with a victory. Thoughts & Observations It’s only three games, so it’s too soon to worry (or celebrate) just about anything, but…I have my eye on Davis’ inefficient offense. He’s been efficient throughout his career and almost certainly will be again. I don’t love the subpar shooting (which might be at least partly attributable to his shot selection) and turnovers. Last night’s game generated a pace factor of 112, which is pretty doggone high. Washington averaged 101.4 possessions per 48 minutes last season. The only game with more possessions was when Bam Adebayo went for 83 points, and there were shenanigans deployed to help him get there. This was the best game of the season for Kyshawn George because of 9 rebounds, 5 assists, and 4 blocks. The offensive efficiency wasn’t there (101 offensive rating — about -10 points per 100 possessions relative to league average), and he did have three turnovers (too many). But he defended without fouling excessively and contributed all over the floor. Bilal Coulibaly is a menace to opposing ball handlers. Or passers. Or those who attempt to shoot near the basket. There’s a not small part of my brain that thinks when the team is playing its most important games this season, the guy who will be out there with Young, Davis, Alex Sarr, and AJ Dybantsa will be Justin Champagnie. He’s tough, physical, and relentless. Last night, he had 14 rebounds in 26 minutes. If Tre Johnson ever finds a magic lamp, I hope he uses one of his wishes on an all-around game. His offensive package looks good, and I think he’s going to be a helluva good shooter. I worry that his lack of non-scoring contributions will keep him nailed to the bench. This was Young’s most in-control and steady all-around game despite getting a technical for flopping. (Which he didn’t deserve, in my opinion. He did fall intentionally, but it looked to me like he was trying to be sure he landed safely with a defender close to him than foul grifting.) Still, 4-10 from deep, 4 rebounds, 9 assists, and just 2 turnovers. Caleb Wilson looks like he’s going to be terrific soon and have a great career. His score in my stat-based pre-draft analysis was consistent with being the No. 1 pick in nearly any draft. It just so happened that he was in a historically good draft, so he landed fourth. I can’t recall the last time I saw one player attempt so many dunks on opponents, and I loved his athleticism, effort, and joy. The biggest thought I had watching him: I can’t wait to see Dybantsa in action. The Chicago Bulls were -21 in Isaac Okoro’s 14 minutes. Just think: The Bulls were +14 in Wilson’s 38 minutes. A bit of math shows the team was -18 in his 10 minutes off the floor. Four Factors Below are the four factors that decide wins and losses in basketball — shooting (efg), rebounding (offensive rebounds), ball handling (turnovers), fouling (free throws made). The four factors are measured by: eFG% (effective field goal percentage, which accounts for the three-point shot) OREB% (offensive rebound percentage) TOV% (turnover percentage — turnovers divided by possessions) FTM/FGA (free throws made divided by field goal attempts) FOUR FACTORS WIZARDS BULLS LGAVG eFG% 53.2% 49.5% 52.4% OREB% 2.8% 19.6% 27.9% TOV% 11.6% 10.7% 14.6% FTM/FGA 0.255 0.301 0.234 PACE 112 101.8 ORTG 111 107 111.1 Stats & Metrics PPA is my overall production metric, which credits players for things they do that help a team win (scoring, rebounding, playmaking, defending) and dings them for things that hurt (missed shots, turnovers, bad defense, fouls). PPA is a per possession metric designed for larger data sets. In small sample sizes, the numbers can get weird. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better and replacement level is 45. For a single game, replacement level isn’t much use, and I reiterate the caution about small samples sometimes producing weird results. POSS is the number of possessions each player was on the floor in this game. ORTG = offensive rating, which is points produced per individual possessions x 100. League average so far this season is listed in the Four Factors table above. Points produced is not the same as points scored. It includes the value of assists and offensive rebounds, as well as sharing credit when receiving an assist. USG = offensive usage rate. Average is 20%. Median so far this season is 17.7%. ORTG and USG are versions of stats created by former Wizards assistant coach Dean Oliver and modified by me. ORTG is an efficiency measure that accounts for the value of shooting, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. USG includes shooting from the floor and free throw line, offensive rebounds, assists and turnovers. +PTS = “Plus Points” is a measure of the points gained or lost by each player based on their efficiency in this game compared to league average efficiency on the same number of possessions. A player with an offensive rating (points produced per possession x 100) of 100 who uses 20 possessions would produce 20 points. If the league average efficiency is 115, the league — on average — would produced 23.0 points in the same 20 possessions. So, the player in this hypothetical would have a +PTS score of -3.0. stories.title: What-If Wolves: Dancing is Forbidden!
stories.summary: The first, and hopefully last, team to break my heart.
stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS - NOVEMBER 26: Kevin Garnett #21 of the Minnesota Timberwolves, Latrell Sprewell #8, and Sam Cassell #19 talk to their head coach Flip Saunders during the game against of the Memphis Grizzlies on November 26, 2004 at the Target Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Timberwolves won 115-90. NOTICE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement: Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2004 NBAE (Photo By David Sherman/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images CONTINUATION OF THE “WHAT IF” WOLVES SERIES . IN THIS SERIES, I PLAY THE ROLE OF TIMBERWOLVES OVERLORD AND GO BACK IN TIME AND RIGHT SOME OF THE WRONGS OF OUR FAVORITE FRANCHISE. SINCE THIS IS THE TIMBERWOLVES, THERE ARE A LOT OF WRONGS. THIS SERIES MAY GO ON FOREVER. “ What If” Wolves Volume 5: From no playoff success to title favorites. This one crushed me. With the addition of LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves, my fandom has gone to another level. A level that I have not experienced since the spring of 2004. Let’s take a trip down the old memory lane for a history lesson on how we could have prevented the biggest heartbreak in my life – well, the biggest heartbreak since I got turned down during the couples skate at CheapSkate way back in the early 90s. The Timberwolves’ first season started in 1989. They were terrible and didn’t even make the playoffs for their first seven seasons. The Wolves’ best record during this stretch was 29-53. 29-53! The first playoff appearance for this woeful franchise came at the end of the 1996-97 season. Kevin Garnett would go on to lead the Wolves to seven straight first-round exits. It was painful. Then the magical 2003-04 season happened. The 2003-04 season was the best time to be a Wolves fan. They finished the season as the best team in the Western Conference with a record of 58-24. KG was named the NBA MVP in a landslide. The roster was much improved with key additions of defensive specialists Trenton Hassell and Ervin Johnson, key bench guys in Fred Hoiberg and Michael Olowakandi, the sharp-shooting Wally Szczerbiak, crazy wing Latrell Sprewell (editor’s note: name your kids after him and they’ll become editors!), and the motor that ran everything, point guard Sam Cassell. Best record, MVP, solid role players, and Flip Saunders doing some coaching magic on a nightly basis. Rolled through the regular season and marched through the playoffs, this team was destined to raise the Larry O’Brien. Then, Sam Cassell decided to do a little dance in honor of Pedro Cerrano and share with everyone that he had the largest cajónes in the NBA. View Link Rumor was that the “Big Balls Dance” that Cassell performed led to a hip avulsion fracture. This “fracture,” along with a previous back injury, caused Sam to miss most of the Western Conference Finals versus the Los Angeles Lakers . Wolves got rinsed in the series 4-2. Title dreams gone. The team would then fall apart, leading to the Wolves missing the playoffs for the next 13 straight seasons. I was absolutely crushed when the Wolves lost to the Lakers. But I can’t wait for Ant and Melo to lead us to the championship (even though they will win it all this year!), so the “What If” Wolves will right this wrong and take away Cassell’s dancing shoes. Like the tiny town in Footloose, dancing is hereby outlawed for this franchise. Not today Mr. Bacon | CBS via Getty Images The real Timberwolves acquired Sam Cassell along with center Ervin Johnson from the Milwaukee Bucks for Anthony Peeler and previous “What If” Wolves subject Joe Smith . Spree was acquired from the Knicks for Terrell Brandon (who would never play ball again due to his knee issues) and Marc Jackson, who would be rerouted to the Philadelphia 76ers . To round out the roster, Trenton Hassell would be signed as a free agent after being waived by the Bulls. This team was a monster. Nobody could score on this group. KG barked defensive orders, and everyone followed along. Hassell lived up to his defensive stopper moniker. Sprewell flew around the court grabbing steals that lead to vicious breakaway dunks. Offensively, they were no slouches either. Cassell ran the show, KG hit turnaround jumper after turnaround jumper, and Fred Hoiberg came off the bench with his form-perfect jump shot. They were top ten in both offense and defensive ratings. Again, this team was a monster. MINNEAPOLIS – FEBRUARY 3: Kevin Garnett #21, Sam Cassell #19 and Latrell Sprewell #8 of the Minnesota Timberwolves goof around on the bench during a game against the Orlando Magic on February 3, 2004 at Target Center in Minneapolis, Minnesota. NOTICE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo By David Sherman/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The regular season was a breeze for this group despite a bunch of injuries to key players in Wally, Troy Hudson, and others. KG finished his MVP year with averages of 24.2 points, 13.9 rebounds, 5 assists, 1.5 steals, and 2.2 blocks. Cassell joined Garnett on the All-Star team. Hoiberg even got some Sixth Man of the Year votes. Previous Wolves teams would have folded in the playoffs. But something about this group was different. The Wolves made quick work of the Denver Nuggets, beating them in 5 games. Cassell (20.6 pts), Sprewell (19.8 pts), and Garnett (25.8 pts, 14.8 rebs, 7 asts) could not be stopped. The Wolves finally won a playoff series. I cannot explain how it felt to finally get a playoff win. It wasn’t excited or joy, mostly just a type of relief. The second round would turn into one of the greatest series in NBA history (don’t argue with me on this one). The Sacramento Kings were the fourth seed, but they were far better than that number suggested. The Kings finished with a 55-27 record. A lot of NBA pundits even thought they could win the whole thing as their roster was stacked with All-Stars, an All-Defensive player, and a crazy solid bench. The series would go back and forth leading up to a historic Game 7. Do yourself a favor and go watch this game right now. KG had a career defining game with 32 points, 21 rebounds, four steals, and five blocks. KG would not be denied in this game. But the Wolves playoff run would be altered in the second game of this series. View Link With just under 30 seconds left in Game 2 , the score is 89-88, Wolves up one. Cassell drives baseline against defensive stalwart Doug Christie, pulls up for his patented mid-range jumper, and nails it. Wolves go up three with 24 seconds left. Sam Cassell is overjoyed and proceeds to do his dance. Cassell scored 59 points in the first two games against the Kings. After the dance, he averaged just 13.2 points per game, with his lowest total of three coming in Game 5. Something wasn’t right with Sam. That’s what happened in real life. But we do revisionist history around here with the “What If” Wolves. Here is how it would have gone down if I was in charge. During the routine physical to complete the trade for Cassell and Johnson, our medical staff discovered that Cassell is running a bit low on testosterone. Now don’t ask me how I know, but increasing your Guy Fuel can have some adverse effects. Cassell was already bald (like me), so no worry about hair loss, but injecting some Power Potion can shrink up your boys (again, don’t ask me how I know this). With Cassell on the gender-affirming treatment to return his testosterone levels to normal, he has been experiencing some shrinkage. Now, of course, Sam still hits that baseline jumper. But instead of attempting his “big balls dance” and possibly causing an injury, Sam simply high fives Ervin Johnson and maybe gets a chest bump from KG. No big balls, no injury. Simple fix. MINNEAPOLIS – MAY 19: Kevin Garnett #21 of the Minnesota Timberwolves acknowledges the crowd after winning Game Seven against the Sacramento Kings in Game Seven of the Western Conference Semifinals during the 2004 NBA Playoffs at Target Center on May 19, 2004 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. NOTICE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement: Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2004 NBAE (Photo by Melissa Majchrzak/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The players and coaches from this Timberwolves squad were all convinced that they would have beaten the Lakers if Cassell wasn’t hurt and I fully agree. The Wolves beat the Lakers three out of four times during the regular season (all wins were by at least 10 points) and had the size in Johnson and Michael Olowokandi to match up with Shaq, and Hassell could limit Kobe somewhat. Conversely, there was nobody on the Lakers who could contain KG or Cassell. LA had Karl Malone and Gary Payton on the team, but both were shells of their former selves. When Cassell went down with his injury in real life, the Wolves were forced to play third-string point guard Darrick Martin, or play Hoiberg out of position. The Wolves even had KG bring the ball up on occasion, which I am sure wore him down a bit. This was an absolute worst-case scenario for the Wolves, but since we have Cassell juicing, the injury from the “Big Balls Dance” never occurred. With a healthy Cassell taking pressure off KG, the “What If” Wolves would defeat the Lakers in five games. Shaq would still have a great series against the Wolves, but he would be the lone bright spot for the Lakers. Kobe Bryant would struggle against the Wolves with Hassell and Sprewell hounding him all series long, plus I am sure that his sexual assault case in Colorado at this time would limit his effectiveness (Kobe would score 42 points against the Spurs after spending all day in court). This loss to the Timberwolves would end up being the true reason why the Lakers broke up the combo of Shaq and Kobe. Lakers destroyed, on to the NBA Finals versus the Detroit Pistons . The Pistons were a great defensive team (second-best in the NBA), led by Defensive Player of the Year winner Ben Wallace, but they truly lacked firepower offensively (18th). I don’t want to dwell on this matchup too much because I believe that this series would have been over in five games. Plus, Coach Flip agreed with me. The lack of offense by the Pistons would be highlighted by the Wolves’ defensive game plan. This Wolves team was just too good on both ends to be denied. KG would go on to win Finals MVP, most likely by averaging a triple-double, and the Wolves would win their first NBA Championship. MINNEAPOLIS – MAY 3: Kevin Garnett #21 of the Minnesota Timberwolves poses for an MVP portrait at Target Center on May 3, 2004 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2004 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images After winning the first championship, free agents would see that the Wolves are no longer the dregs of the NBA and start to see Minnesota as a great destination. The Timberwolves go on to win title after title. Sprewell still would leave in the offseason so he could “feed his family”. Cassell finishes his career with the Wolves and takes over as head coach when Flip retires. KG continues to dominate the league, finishes his career in “Minny,” his jersey gets put up in the rafters, and a statue of him dunking on the Kings’ Brad Miller from Game 7 sits outside of Target Center. Hell, maybe a second statue of him yelling at a teammate gets put up at the practice facility. After all, he is the new owner of the Wolves, so he can do whatever he wants as long as nobody dances.

stories.title: Turnovers continue to plague the Cavs in the fourth quarter
stories.summary: “There’s no excuses, but we are working on it,”
stories.detailText: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 24: Tyrese Proctor #24 listens to Donovan Mitchell #45 of the Cleveland Cavaliers during the fourth quarter against the Brooklyn Nets at Rocket Arena on October 24, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. The Cavs defeated the Nets 125-121. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images CLEVELAND — The Cleveland Cavaliers have lost the two fourth quarters they’ve played this season by a combined 24 points. Their poor late-game execution kept them from delivering a statement win over the Philadelphia 76ers on opening night, and it almost cost them again two days later in their home opener against the Brooklyn Nets . The culprit behind both collapses was the same. “We lost the possession game by 16,” head coach Kenny Atkinson said after his team narrowly defeated the Nets . “We got to clean up the turnovers.” Turnovers lead to bad offense. Bad offense leads to bad defense. You combine those together, and 22-point leads can evaporate in a heartbeat , even against an inexperienced Nets team. “Good offense [is important] because it really helps you guard the ball,” Mario Hezonja said. “Our rhythm is imposed onto the opponent, so it’s much easier to go both ways. The moment you start to have bad turnovers or bad possessions or even bad shots…that impacts a lot of the mental aspect for a player, and it impacts a lot of the defensive side.” It’s easy to look at the poor fourth quarter in Game 1 last postseason against the New York Knicks and the start of this season, and believe that there’s a mental barrier keeping the Cavs from closing out games. Maybe there is, but at least in these first two games, the Cavs’ issues are very much basketball-related. As was the case in Philadelphia, the Cavs once again struggled to handle ball pressure. It’s a copycat league. Teams see what works, and then try to replicate it. One wave we’re seeing now is a drastic increase in blitzing defenses. Defenses are more aggressive in how they’re sending doubles and jumping passing lanes than before. That is especially true late in games, when opponents are trailing and are desperate to get back into games. Hence the reason the Cavs are struggling with this so much down the stretch. “There’s an unpredictability to it,” Donovan Mitchell said. “I think it’s random. The NBA has turned into that as a whole. Indiana really did a great job of it two years ago, and I think everybody followed suit. It was just like, just cause chaos and figure it out. … When you’re picking up full court and randomly trapping, there’s really no scheme for that. It’s like AAU basketball.” Atkinson has emphasized the need to just “ pass to the open man .” That sounds simple enough and is what needs to happen. The problems come when the team isn’t currently capable of doing that. There are a couple of issues preventing the Cavs from doing so. First, their starting lineup only has two players they trust to operate in these situations with the ball in their hands. Second, there isn’t a good feel for where guys should be on the court when the traps come. “It’s a different five,” Mitchell said. “[We’re] calling different plays.” For as frustrating as these first two games have been, the sky isn’t falling — at least not yet. These are things that can be cleaned up. “There’s no excuses, but we are working on it,” Hezonja said. “There are some new pieces that we added to the team, so this unfortunately takes a little bit of time, but we are working on it. Everything started to mesh better and better, and I hope [that] soon it’s going to look good.” Time is on the Cavs’ side. The regular season is where you build habits and problem-solve for how teams are going to attack you. Right now, the book is out on how to disrupt the Cavs: be physical with them at the point of attack and send random double teams at their guards. That is how teams will defend them until the Cavs show they can beat that kind of defense. And from a certain perspective, going through these struggles now instead of in April should benefit them. “It’s not always going to be perfect,” Mitchell said, “but I think for us, having these first two games…similar but different ways, I think is definitely going to help us in the long run.”

stories.title: What is Joe Mazzulla’s rotation telling us after two games?
stories.summary: Eleven Celtics have played. The minutes are already offering clues about who Joe Mazzulla trusts the most.
stories.detailText: Oct 23, 2026; Boston, Massachusetts, USA; As the bench celebrates, Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla watches the play during the second half against the New York Knicks at TD Garden. Mandatory Credit: Winslow Townson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Joe Mazzulla has used 11 players in each of the Celtics’ first two games, which sounds democratic until you inspect the timecards. Everybody has checked in, but that doesn’t mean everybody has a full-time job. Jayson Tatum, Derrick White and Paul George have predictably played the most. Payton Pritchard is fourth in total minutes despite coming off the bench. Sam Hauser has logged more minutes than Jordan Walsh and Mitchell Robinson, two members of the starting lineup. Hugo González has played just 13 minutes. Two games are not enough to settle Boston’s rotation, but they do give us some clues about how Mazzulla is sorting it. The same five players started against Detroit and New York : White, George, Tatum, Walsh and Mitchell Robinson. Everything after that has been more fluid. The first week has already exposed a few levels of trust. Pritchard’s bench designation looks increasingly cosmetic. Hauser may be the cleanest solution to Boston’s spacing issues. Among the young wings, meanwhile, the minutes have not been distributed equally. Here are my biggest takeaways from Joe’s rotations through the first two games. Boston, MA – October 14: Boston Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla talks to guards Derrick White and Payton Pritchard in the second quarter. The Boston Celtics played the Charlotte Hornets in a preseason game at TD Garden on October 14, 2026. (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Pritchard is a bench player in name only Pritchard explained his definition of a starter after practice last Sunday. “To me, a starter is the amount of minutes you play,” he said. “Do you finish games? Are you playing 30-plus minutes? Then you are a starter.” By his own math, Pritchard is starting. He has played 57 minutes and 56 seconds through two games. Only Tatum, White and George have played more. Against the Knicks, Pritchard scored a measly four points on 1-for-6 shooting, but still remained on the floor for more than 30 minutes. I’m not going to try and spin his four points as a secretly great performance. He missed five of his six shots and never found an offensive rhythm. But cold shooting nights can reveal more about a coach’s confidence than another three-point avalanche. Any reasonable person would leave Pritchard on the floor while he’s setting fire to the net. Mazzulla stayed with him even when he wasn’t. Single-game plus-minus can tell lies with a straight face, but Boston still outscored New York by eight points during Pritchard’s 30 minutes. It wasn’t Pritchard’s night, but it wasn’t a problem large enough to lose a game, which is probably the distinction Mazzulla cares about most. The Celtics opened the second quarter with Pritchard, White, George, Hauser and Luka Garza. Tatum rested while George carried the star responsibilities. Boston started the fourth with almost the same construction, swapping Robinson in for Garza. Pritchard was the constant. He is becoming the connective tissue between Boston’s different versions of itself. Incredible early offense from Boston Ghost screen by Hauser gets him to the top then we see Stagger screen for Pritchard Only needed the one from George here pic.twitter.com/KtUzWo5Sox — Nik Land | NikNBA🏀 (@NIKNBAYT) October 23, 2026 His closing role was more situational. Mazzulla initially went with Tatum, George, White, Hauser and Queta during crunch time. Pritchard returned for Hauser with 1:11 remaining, giving Boston another ball handler and free-throw shooter. He made one at the line, then was replaced by Queta for the final defensive possession. That wasn’t one permanent closing five we saw Friday night. Mazzulla was changing the group possession by possession, which is probably how this roster should work. Pritchard may not always be standing on the court when the game ends, but he’s made it clear that he’ll be plenty involved in getting Boston there. Hauser keeps solving lineup problems Hauser has played 40 minutes and 52 seconds, six seconds more than Robinson. That isn’t a meaningful statistical gap, but it’s a pretty useful reminder of how little the starting label matters to Mazzulla. He has made five of his first 10 three-point attempts after shooting 39.3% from deep last season, the worst mark of his career and still a percentage most players would happily tell their grandkids about down the road. His shooting stretches the floor in ways Boston needs, particularly when Mazzulla uses Queta or Robinson at center. Those big men provide vertical spacing, offensive rebounding and rim protection. Neither one is naturally dragging a defender away from the paint. Hauser gives those groups oxygen. The best example came against Detroit. White, Hauser, Tatum, George and Queta turned a 39-39 game into a 57-43 Celtics lead in roughly five minutes. That lineup produced a 172.7 offensive rating and a 136.4 net rating, which are hilarious numbers that should not be treated as remotely sustainable. The part worth taking seriously was the fit. Four shooters surrounding Queta gave everyone room to operate. Mazzulla returned to the same idea against New York. George was getting ready to set this pin down for Hauser but he rejects it seeing PG had the mismatch NYK doubles and Hauser sets screen for Pritchard to go to corner and McBride follows – Hauser open 3 pic.twitter.com/y7KEhBVBHE — Nik Land | NikNBA🏀 (@NIKNBAYT) October 24, 2026 Hauser opened the fourth quarter alongside Robinson, Pritchard, White and George. Later, with the Knicks threatening, Mazzulla used Hauser next to Queta in a lineup with Tatum, George and White. The shooting explains why Hauser fits, but his defense might be why Mazzulla can keep turning to him. Hauser still gets hunted occasionally because opposing stars see a white guy with a sensible haircut and make certain assumptions. Those assumptions have not produced easy baskets as often as expected. According to NBA tracking data from last season , opponents shot 0.7 percentage points below their expected field-goal percentage when Hauser was the closest defender. He is sturdy enough to survive switches, rarely wanders away from the scheme and has become good at forcing scorers into shots the defense can live with. Nobody is asking him to turn into Scottie Pippen. He just can’t be the loose thread every offense tries to pull. That combination of competent defense and elite shooting allows Mazzulla to place him almost anywhere without creating an obvious problem at either end. Queta did make his only three-point attempt against New York, so Hauser should probably keep an eye on his job. Queta is currently shooting 100% from deep, and I refuse to entertain any small-sample-size arguments at this time. Until Queta starts receiving the same treatment behind the arc, Hauser gives Mazzulla a proven shooter without handing opposing offenses an obvious place to attack. The young wings are not receiving equal auditions Walsh, Scheierman, González and Ron Harper Jr. entered the season as Boston’s collection of young wings. The first two games have not treated them as interchangeable. Walsh has started both games and played 33 minutes and 45 seconds. His offense remains a work in progress, but Mazzulla has given him difficult defensive assignments, including Cade Cunningham in Detroit and Jalen Brunson against the Knicks, and allowed him to play through mistakes. He also rewarded that patience against New York, hitting a three and scoring on a nice cut during Boston’s third-quarter run. I asked Paul George what he saw from Jordan Walsh against Jalen Brunson tonight and how, when Walsh was matched up with him, that freed George to be a defensive playmaker off the ball. “I thought he was special. I thought he set the tone.” https://t.co/7XYsM54Mq8 pic.twitter.com/OqPLLAr0vx — Bobby Krivitsky (@BobbyKrivitsky) October 24, 2026 Scheierman has played 29 minutes and 22 seconds. He scored eight points in the opener, made both of his threes and already looks more willing to make a quick decision when the ball finds him. Mazzulla has used him in both halves of both games, including alongside Tatum during the third quarter Friday. González has played just 13 minutes and 18 seconds. Only Garza has played fewer. Harper has yet to see the floor at all. González checked in midway through the first quarter against New York, stayed on the court for three minutes and 35 seconds and never returned. His 13 total minutes are less than half of Scheierman’s and well below Walsh’s. That isn’t a verdict on a 20-year-old two games into his second NBA season. González had a really encouraging preseason, and his size, defensive instincts and fearlessness should get him onto the court plenty as the season wears on. Boston’s first back-to-back arrives Monday and Tuesday, which may create an opportunity almost immediately. For now, Mazzulla appears more comfortable with Walsh’s defense and Scheierman’s…Scheiermanning. The gap is worth noticing without declaring it permanent. These first two games show Mazzulla’s initial preferences with a healthy roster. They don’t tell us what the rotation will look like after a difficult back-to-back, an injury or the first time somebody ahead of González stops giving the Celtics what they need. Garza provided a useful reminder that the bottom of the rotation can still change quickly. He entered against New York, scored eight points in three and a half minutes, made two threes, drew a charge and returned to the bench like a man who had broken into the game, emptied the register and disappeared before anyone could identify him. Great opening sequence by Luka Garza Steal on defense as he plays the Spain perfectly then hits the corner three after the Tatum timely pass Just drew a charge too pic.twitter.com/U0NvIDHscp — Nik Land | NikNBA🏀 (@NIKNBAYT) October 23, 2026 Garzilla behavior. Mazzulla will need those little bursts over 82 games, but every player producing one doesn’t suddenly move into the permanent rotation. Right now, Walsh and Scheierman have the longer runway. González is waiting for his next opening. Harper is waiting for his first. Tatum and George are sharing the floor, and the workload The Celtics did not acquire George so he and Tatum could alternate isolations while everyone else watched. Through two games, Mazzulla has started working on a more useful kind of staggering. Against the Knicks, Tatum rested to begin the second quarter while George played with Pritchard, White, Hauser and Garza. Tatum played the entire third, with George sitting for the final four and a half minutes. George then opened the fourth while Tatum rested. At the 6:53 mark, Tatum replaced George. Just over two minutes later, George returned and the two stars finished the game together. The basic rhythm is beginning to emerge. Tatum and George overlap at the beginning and end of halves, then take turns anchoring the middle. Pritchard moves between both groups. White can run the offense with either. Hauser gives each of them another outlet when the defense loads up. The arrangement should keep Boston from living through too many possessions without a high-level creator. It also gives George stretches where he can operate as the primary option instead of trying to fit his touches around Tatum’s. welcome YEAR 10 JAYSON TATUM 🥹 pic.twitter.com/GuA71oe1uR — Tomek Kordylewski (@Timi_093) October 24, 2026 There will be nights when the rotation gets smaller. Injuries, foul trouble and matchups will rearrange all of this. If we have learned anything about Mazzulla, it’s that he will happily abandon Tuesday’s rotation by Thursday and seem mildly irate that anyone expected otherwise. Still, his first two games have given us a working hierarchy. Tatum, White and George are the foundation. Pritchard is a starter, his words, not mine. Hauser and the two centers give Mazzulla different ways to build around them. Walsh and Scheierman have received meaningful auditions. González, Garza and Harper are waiting for the game that calls for them. There are still 80 games left. Roles will change, new lineups will emerge and Mazzulla may render half of this article obsolete by Thanksgiving. For now, we get to study two games far more closely than any reasonable person should, because Celtics basketball is finally back.

teamStories.detailText: DALLAS, TX - OCTOBER 24: Stephon Castle #5 of the San Antonio Spurs dunks the ball during the game against the Dallas Mavericks on October 24, 2026 at American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Glenn James/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images With 5:53 left in the second quarter, Dallas Mavericks center Daniel Gafford grabbed an offensive rebound, dunked it home, and screamed at his home crowd. The energy play gave the Mavs a 49-43 lead, despite missing several key starters like Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving. That play prompted a timeout from San Antonio Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson. At that point, all of the doom and gloom about the Spurs’ first two games seemed warranted. The team looked sluggish and disengaged in a genuinely worrisome way. What happened to the fire and spunk this team played with last season? Johnson may have asked them the same question in the huddle during that second-quarter timeout. A different team emerged from the bench after the pep talk. San Antonio responded with a 25-11 run after the timeout, leading to their first win of the season, 122-106. So what changed after that point? It started with defensive pressure at the point of attack. Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell, and De’Aaron Fox all had multiple steals as the team forced 21 turnovers, leading to 26 points off them. The energy and intensity on defense changed after the timeout. The Mavericks’ backcourt mistakes led to easy runouts for the Spurs, igniting a scoring explosion that inevitably won the game. Just a tweak in intensity and aggression made a major difference on the scoreboard. To start the season, San Antonio’s players and coaches have talked a lot about effort and focus. Fox cited a bad preseason, and Mitch Johnson talked about playing up to a standard and not being a team that just flips the effort switch on and off. It’s concerning that a team coming off an NBA Finals in which they blew multiple winnable games is still showing inconsistent effort. But maybe a dominant win against a team they are supposed to beat will wake them up from this early-season stupor. San Antonio is entering an easier part of their early-season schedule with games against teams that failed to make the playoffs last year. Some dominant wins would be the type of continued response this team needs, and could signal this game as a turning point for this year’s squad. Takeaways: San Antonio is still struggling to figure out its new rotation. The four-guard starting lineup has forced Johnson to change how he staggers his guards. The results thus far have been mixed. The starting lineup has a +1.8 net rating in 28 minutes, with the defense looking great and the offense shaky. Johnson has then taken Fox out first and brought him back in to run the second unit with Keldon Johnson, Julian Champagnie, Carter Bryant/Harrison Barnes, and Luke Kornet. Small sample size here, but that lineup has a net rating of -77.8 in 9 minutes. The group simply needs more playmaking to succeed. It ultimately turns into Fox dominating the ball with limited movement, and no offensive flow. The bench lineup was on the floor for most of Dallas’ scoring runs on Saturday. Part of what has made those second-unit lineups look so bad, and what killed San Antonio in the playoffs last year, has been the play of Kornet. Plus-minus is not usually a great stat, but it can be helpful when it matches the eye test. Kornet was -18 in 14 minutes, going 0-2 from the field, grabbing 4 rebounds and recording 2 turnovers. He has not finished in the paint, nor protected the rim well to start this season. His offensive limitations are exacerbated by the Spurs’ lack of second-unit creation, and if he’s not crushing the glass or holding down the paint, it’s hard to find a lot of positives in having him out there. With Kornet struggling, the Spurs went to the rookie, Tarris Reed, to start the third quarter. The rookie helped the team go on an 11-4 run in his 4-minute stint. Reed scored his first NBA bucket on a lob from Vassell, and snatched an offensive rebound that eventually led to a Champagnie three-pointer. He had 2 points, 3 rebounds, and a turnover in 7 total minutes. That performance, and Kornet’s struggles, should earn the rookie some more minutes moving forward. We’ll see if the coaching staff gradually increases his opportunities as they did for Bryant last season. Victor Wembanyama had a much better game by keeping things simple against Dallas. He led the team in scoring with 23 points on 9-for-18 shooting, making 2 of his 6 three-pointers. He mainly served as a lob threat in the pick-and-roll, particularly thriving when running the action with Fox. He still took some frustrating three-pointers, but the ones he made genuinely came within the flow of the offense. He was also one of the players who benefitted from Johnson’s second-quarter pep talk. Wembanyama looked a step slow and lethargic in the first half, but responded with improved defense in the second. It was a step in the right direction, but we still haven’t seen Wembanyama put it all together this season. Fox was the Spurs MVP on Saturday night. He had 19 points on 6-for-11 shooting, adding 9 assists and 3 steals. He was fantastic in the pick-and-roll, developing chemistry with Wembanyama. He’s taking and making shots within the flow of the offense. He may be thriving more than any of Spur in these new guard-heavy lineups. Castle’s shooting may be real. The third-year guard is now shooting 37.9% from three on 9.7 attempts to start the season. He went 3-for-8 from deep on Saturday. Teams are leading him open for the most part, and he still struggles to shoot threes off the dribble, but when his feet are set, his shot looks good. If he becomes a 36%+ shooter this season, he’ll make it easier for the Spurs to play him alongside Harper and Fox. Keldon Johnson was back to playing the high-energy role that made him so successful last season. He had 7 points and 6 rebounds, 4 of them offensive, in his 26 minutes. Johnson continues to be at his best when he is driving hard to the cup in transition and crashing the boards.

teamStories.detailText: DALLAS, TX - OCTOBER 24: Devin Vassell #24 of the San Antonio Spurs drives to the basket during the game against the Dallas Mavericks on October 24, 2026 at American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Cooper Neill/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It wasn’t the prettiest of performances, but a few great defensive stretches were enough to give the Spurs their first win of the season. The production from the starters was simply impossible for a Mavericks team missing Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving to match, as San Antonio pulled away late en route to a 122-106 victory on the road. While they had some dominant moments in the second half, the winless Spurs didn’t look as hungry as expected early on, showing both a lack of execution that wasn’t surprising from a tired team in the second game of a back-to-back, but also lacking the sense of urgency of a contender that lost a tough game the night before should show. Fortunately, they were facing a shorthanded opponent who had also played on Friday, so even during the sloppy moments, they stayed close on the scoreboard. Aside from a few good stretches from Stephon Castle and Devin Vassell, who took advantage of a zone defense by hitting midrange jumpers, there wasn’t much that stood out from a seemingly uninspired San Antonio squad in the opening frame. Despite missing their two best players, the Mavericks didn’t struggle to keep it close. The lack of hustle plays, the poor decision-making that led to opponent fastbreak points, and the lazy defense that led to fouling were still there in the second quarter. The Mavs were getting help from their bench guys, especially Sergio De Larrea, while the Spurs were struggling to find a spark. An 8-2 run from the home team, punctuated by a big dunk by Daniel Gafford off an offensive rebound, allowed them to create some separation, and the concerns about the matchup turning into a trap game were starting to creep in. The timeout that followed that play changed everything. Whatever Mitch Johnson said worked, because the focus and the energy improved massively, especially from Victor Wembanyama, who didn’t look like himself earlier. San Antonio played harder and, thanks to their superior talent, went on a 25-11 run to close the half. After the break, the Spurs seemed determined to turn the game into a blowout. The defense was creating turnovers or missed shots, and the Mavericks didn’t have any answers. Unfortunately, the execution just wasn’t good enough on the offensive end, neither in transition nor in the half-court, to truly pull away. The Silver and Black did secure a double-digit lead, but it didn’t last long. As the starters went to the bench, the second unit struggled to keep up the defensive pressure, and De’Aaron Fox couldn’t carry the offense by himself. The buffer that took so much effort to create disappeared quickly, as the Mavericks won the frame and trailed by just three heading into the final period. San Antonio still looked in control, but it felt like the Spurs had let the opportunity to walk away with an easy win pass. A dominant fourth quarter showed that, while the floor of the team is not where it’s supposed to be, as Mitch Johnson said postgame, this version of the Silver and Black still has a high ceiling that it can reach when necessary, even when unfamiliar faces are asked to contribute. Tarris Reed Jr. got his first NBA minutes, showing that the coaching staff was looking for energy wherever it could find it, and the rookie responded. Unlike the rest of the game, the team didn’t desperately need Wembanyama when he was resting, and when the Alien returned to the court, the lead had actually grown to nine points. Great defense, timely outside shots, and a good stretch from Wemby sealed the win. It was arguably later than it should have been, but San Antonio got to rest its rotation players for the last three minutes, on their way to emerging victorious for the first time this season. Play of the game De’Aaron Fox and Victor Wembanyama are finally developing more chemistry in the pick-and-roll, which is a joy to watch. W🤯W! 📺 @_daznus pic.twitter.com/1pBdI0MCC5 — San Antonio Spurs (@spurs) October 25, 2026 Game notes: It was not a particularly good night for Wembanyama, despite what his impressive stat line in 29 minutes might suggest. Wemby has not looked as dominant as in past seasons so far and was subtly called out by Mitch Johnson for a lack of effort postgame. The Spurs still outscored the Mavericks by 32 points when he was on the floor, because his impact is almost always massive even when he doesn’t look spectacular, but we’ve still haven’t seen the real Wemby so far this season. De’Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle had remarkably similar stat lines, as they both finished with 19 points, three rebounds and three steals, while Fox had one more assist (nine) than the young guard. Both made their mark on defense at times, and while the veteran balanced scoring and playmaking better, the two were essential at different stretches on offense. The other two starters switched roles for one night. Devin Vassell had six assists (and no turnovers) but only hit one of his outside shots. Harper only had two assists, but he hit three outside shots. As long as the production is there, it doesn’t really matter who does what. Julian Champagnie and Keldon Johnson provided defense, some scoring, and much-needed energy off the bench, but the second unit wasn’t great as a whole. The lineups that feature Fox and four subs put too much pressure on the point guard to create and be the main point-of-attack defender, so Mitch Johnson might need to find a new strategy if the struggles continue. Relatedly, the decision to go with Reed Jr. in the fourth showed that the coaching staff is not actually scared to make tweaks when needed. Luke Kornet has had a rough start to the season and was terrible in Dallas, so the rookie got some minutes. Reed’s defense isn’t polished, but his rebounding and physicality should make him an alternative when the other option isn’t working out. Next game: vs. Sacramento Kings on Tuesday The schedule gets even softer for the Spurs, which should be 2-2 after hosting the lowly Kings, as long as they take them seriously enough.

teamStories.detailText: DALLAS, TX - OCTOBER 24: Zaccharie Risacher #10 of the Dallas Mavericks looks to pass the ball during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on October 24, 2026 at American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Glenn James/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The Dallas Mavericks played their first of 16 back-to-backs Saturday night, losing to the Spurs, 122-106 . With Cooper Flagg sidelined due to a shoulder injury and Kyrie Irving getting some load management rest, there was plenty of opportunity for others to shine against the Western Conference reigning champions. 5-for-5: Dusty May on Coach’s Challenges Dusty May has a keen knack for spotting referee errors. A Coach’s Challenge early in the second quarter overturned a foul call on Daniel Gafford. That prevented Gafford from picking up his third foul, allowed the Mavericks to maintain possession and kept May flawless on Coach’s Challenges for the season. He did it again in the third quarter on an out-of-bounds call to once again get possession back to the Mavs. He has now challenged five times this season and won all five of them. It may seem a bit trivial, and he surely won’t maintain 100% success all season, but this should not be overlooked. Possessions add up over the season and not burning timeouts are the little things that matter in the game of inches. 25-10: Spurs’ second-chance points advantage Dallas played hard all night, but that effort still saw them come up short on the boards. The Spurs did well to pursue the ball off the glass, giving themselves second chance points aplenty. On a few occasions, the Mavs’ secured the rebound only to turn it over, netting the same result as giving up an offensive board in the first place. Daniel Gafford’s foul trouble didn’t help the cause, but the Mavs are going to need to collectively swarm the boards to remedy the early-season trend of getting out-rebounded. Putting it mildly, Dallas got smoked in this department by a factor of two-and-a-half times. 9-of-15: Sergio De Larrea FG shooting For a guy who looked largely out of sorts during his first two NBA games, to look like a seasoned NBA player against one of the best teams in the league, is quite impressive. De Larrea was unconscious on the offensive end. A huge worry coming into the game was the absence of Irving and who would fill his role. Hall of Famers are not easily replaceable on a given night, but De Larrea did his best to at least provide scoring punch with a bit of offensive orchestration peppered in. If this is De Larrea’s arrival, we’re in for a treat the rest of the way. He led all Mavericks in scoring with 21 points. 14: Number of Dallas Stocks The Mavericks’ defensive effort has added up to a high stocks (steals + blocks) total over the past two games. Saturday night saw another admirable number posted. In and of itself, it’s nice to see, however the real story is more often what that defensive effort amounts to. In this case, Dallas dominated on fast break points, 28 to 15. Having gotten badly beaten on second chance points, Dallas needed to make up for that deficit somewhere and the defensive combination of steals and blocks was where they did it. I invite you to follow me @_80MPH on X, and check back often at Mavs Moneyball for all the latest on the Dallas Mavericks.

stories.title: Colts doomed for fire sale after suffering third straight loss to Vikings
stories.summary: It felt like another cruel reminder of how badly it has unraveled as the Colts have earned as many wins overseas between Berlin and London as they have stateside over the past calendar year.
stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Minnesota Vikings defensive end Dallas Turner #15 and safety Harrison Smith #22 sack Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones #17 in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium — October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images An inspired defensive effort gave the offense every opportunity to leave Minnesota with a victory Sunday, but an absent passing attack, two rarely missed field goals and another deciding turnover delivered a familiar defeat. The Colts lost 16-10 to the Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium, dropping their third straight game and falling to 2-5 this season. Indianapolis led 10-6 at halftime, but could not engineer any points in the second half. It felt like another cruel reminder of how badly it has unraveled as the Colts have earned as many wins overseas between Berlin and London as they have stateside over the past calendar year. Daniel Jones finished 13 of 22 for just 108 passing yards, throwing his seventh decisive interception to end the final drive. The Colts entered Sunday with a minus-8 turnover margin, which was the worst in the NFL. Minnesota averaged a league-high two takeaways per game, and Indianapolis lost the turnover battle again, on the final chance to win the game. The defense did enough to win and Taylor showcased he can still generate the most explosive play of the game. But when the offense scores just 10 points, the glaring missed field goals and mistakes to close the game cost the Colts another game. The Colts did not need perfection Sunday, but they needed their offense to finish drives. Perhaps the biggest issue with backup QB Anthony Richardson Sr. was his inability to sustain drives, but it’s near malpractice not to include a package for the dual-threat QB to play snaps inside the red zone. Jaylahn Tuimoloau and Akeem Davis-Gaither stuffed Vikings running back Aaron Jones in the backfield on fourth down to force a turnover on downs on their opening drive. Indianapolis broke the ice as Daniel Jones relied on his security blanket to move the chains. Facing third down, Jones hit receiver Keenan Allen on a slant to move the sticks near midfield. Three plays later, Jones motioned Josh Downs across the formation and found his slot receiver on a hitch to convert another third down. Star running back Jonathan Taylor took over from there with the longest play from scrimmage, breaking through the Vikings touted defense for a 38-yard touchdown run to cap a seven-play, 61-yard opening drive to give Indianapolis an early 7-0 lead. Taylor led the Colts with 110 scrimmage yards, including 95 rushing yards on 18 carries and one touchdown. Jonathan Taylor breaks through! 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/lcFr4An7JV — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 25, 2026 The defense had opportunities to get stops as Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell was aggressive with two early tries on fourth down. Quarterback Kyler Murray moved the Vikings into scoring range three times in the first half, but Indianapolis forced Minnesota to settle for a pair of field goals as Will Reichard connected from 28 and 47 yards out on consecutive drives to cut the deficit to 7-6. Aside from the missed opportunities on special teams, the two most costly sequences for the Colts were clearly the end of each half. Indianapolis appeared poised to extend its lead with the offense set up five yards from the end zone with goal-to-go inside the final minute of the first half. An offensive holding penalty pushed the Colts backward, then Jones took an inexcusable 11-yard sack on second down that let the game clock wind down. Spencer Shrader salvaged the 22-play drive with a 43-yard field goal as time expired to give the Colts a 10-6 lead at halftime. The second half was a much different story for Shrader. He missed wide left on a tough 56-yarder that wasted a 13-play drive, then missed a 48-yarder wide right that squandered a chance to level the score late in the final frame. Minnesota’s pass rush overwhelmed Indianapolis, gathering consecutive sacks to force a punt that flipped field position. Shrader’s first miss proved costly on the first play of the fourth quarter when Murray opened with a 35-yard scramble. Murray found tight end T.J. Hockenson at the near pylon for a 5-yard touchdown to take a 13-10 lead. The Colts answered with another four-minute drive into Vikings territory, only to settle for a chance to tie and watched Shrader miss a 48-yard field goal wide right with just 4:27 left to play. When the league-leading scorer leaves six points on the field, it was no secret that this game was slipping out of reach. To give credit where it’s due, Indianapolis refused to fold as defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore delivered a breakout performance with five tackles and two sacks, including a key takedown of Murray late in the fourth. Needing a stop to stay within striking distance, cornerback Kenneth Harris also stepped up and broke up a pass to force Reichard to settle for a field goal from 52 yards with 1:39 remaining. Tomi does it again 💥 📺 CBS pic.twitter.com/5Lvz0Q3UiG — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 25, 2026 The Colts still had one final chance to drive down the field against a Minnesota defense that had not allowed a fourth-quarter touchdown all season. Jones opened the final possession with a 15-yard completion to Downs, giving Indianapolis a lifeline. Then Jones lofted his second pass over the middle, where veteran safety Harrison Smith was waiting to jump the route and picked it off, terminating the final drive and sealing Minnesota’s sixth-straight victory. The rivalry victory over Houston offered a brief reprieve, but Indianapolis has dropped to 2-5, still searching for answers after a change in the front office. With three straight losses and the lack of consistency on either side of the ball, the pressure on Coach Shane Steichen only intensified.Indianapolis needs its kicker to deliver and its franchise quarterback to make a play when the game is on the line, but right now, even that seems like just too much to ask for an organization on the cusp of a fire sale.

stories.title: Aaron Glenn: Disappointed in myself, but totally believe we're on the right track
stories.summary: The Jets fell to 2-5 on Sunday by losing 28-25 at home to a previously winless Dolphins team that took a 21-7 halftime lead and then held on in the second half of the game.
stories.detailText: The Jets fell to 2-5 on Sunday by losing 28-25 at home to a previously winless Dolphins team that took a 21-7 halftime lead and then held on in the second half of the game. After the game, head coach Aaron Glenn said he was "disappointed in myself first and foremost" because of the way the defense failed to perform in the first half of the game. Glenn calls the plays on that side of the ball and nothing he did worked out until the Jets were trying to dig themselves out of a hole. They held the Dolphins at bay long enough to cut the lead to four points in the fourth quarter, but then gave up a 63-yard touchdown and failed to stop Miami on a late fourth down that sealed the win for the road team. Glenn pointed to that second half life as reason to believe that he has the Jets moving in the right direction. "I would say yes. The reason why I would say that is cause there’s no quit in these guys," Glenn said at his press conference. "I know what the record is, I do, but I know what I feel about these players and how hard these players play. Come out the second half, it was probably doom and gloom from everything outside of it. But inside this locker room, the guys were ready to go and I think they showed up. I know that we're not where we need to be, but I totally believe that we're on the right track." Glenn went on to say that it's been seven games and that the Jets have "a number of games left and that’s how we look at it." The truth is that the Jets are now 5-20 since Glenn became their head coach and there's no sign of the kind of consistency and execution needed to build a sustained winner under his watch. Whether or not a loss to the 0-5 Dolphins becomes the point of no return for his tenure will be up to Jets owner Woody Johnson.

stories.title: Is Taylor Swift at the Chiefs game tonight? Status for Week 7 vs. Seahawks
stories.summary: The Chiefs are so far 3-0 in matchups Swift has attended this season, but the superstar rarely makes public appearances at road games.
stories.detailText: Taylor Swift has been a fixture at Kansas City Chiefs home games since she began dating tight end Travis Kelce in 2023, but the pop superstar has been less likely to show up – at least publicly – at road games. That puts her status up in the air for the Chiefs biggest road test of the 2026 season so far. Undefeated Kansas City (5-0) will travel to Seattle (3-3) in Week 7 to face the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks in a "Sunday Night Football" matchup. Seattle, which enters the prime-time showdown having lost three of their last four games, will hope to get their season back on track with a win over Kansas City. Will a matchup of recent NFL heavyweights be enough to draw Swift to the Pacific Northwest? Here's what we know: Is Taylor Swift at the Chiefs game today? Keeping with tradition, Taylor Swift has attended each of the Chiefs' home games so far this season, and she's had some famous faces by her side. We don't know yet if she'll make her first road game appearance of the season on Sunday, Oct. 25, when the Chiefs travel to Seattle for "SNF." This story will be updated when we know more. Swift, who married Kelce in the offseason, watched the Chiefs defeat the Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium in Week 1 with Hollywood superstar Tom Cruise in her usual suite . She also was on hand for K.C.'s win over the Colts on "Sunday Night Football" in Week 2. Kelce led the Chiefs in receiving yards and was tied for the team lead in catches against the Broncos in the victory, with a vintage 101-yard performance coming in Week 2. After a pair of road wins in Miami and Las Vegas, Swift watched the Chiefs and Kelce win on their home turf with a Week 6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. This time she was joined by WNBA star Caitlin Clark , and Kelce had four catches for 53 yards. Historically, the future Hall of Famer has performed well with Swift in attendance.
